div.p: The Simple MDA tool answers one question about one gamma line: given this spectrum, this detector response, and this distance, how much of the nuclide could be present without you having seen it? It reports an upper limit at a confidence level you choose, and if there is a detectable excess it reports that instead.

Currie sums the counts in a region around the peak and compares them with what the channels on either side predict. It makes no assumption about peak shape, which makes it robust and easy to check by hand, and it is the method the ISO 11929 and Currie-style conventions describe.

Deconvolution instead fits a peak of the expected shape and width at a range of trial source strengths, and finds the strength at which the fit becomes inconsistent with the data. Because it uses the peak shape, it can do better where the gross-counts assumption breaks down — a sloping continuum, or a neighbouring peak that is itself in the fit. It depends on the detector response being right, and on its own background model matching the data: the continuum is a straight line unless you choose otherwise.
When the two disagree substantially, that usually says something about the data rather than about the methods: most often a curved continuum under the peak, or an interfering line in the region.
The deconvolution method exposes two options that are easy to confuse, because they sound similar but answer different questions.

ul.li: Continuum treatment ("Cont. Norm") — where the knowledge of the background under the peak comes from. Covered in detail below.

Background reference — which measurement the limit is about. Leave it unchecked and the limit bounds the signal in the spectrum you have. Check it and you are asserting this spectrum contains no signal, and asking what a future measurement would be able to detect. That result is a predicted sensitivity, not a bound on the spectrum in hand, and is reported as such.

div.p: The mechanical difference is small; the difference in what you are claiming is not. It comes down to where the knowledge of the background comes from.

ul.li: Floating infers the background from the same channels that might contain the signal. You assert nothing about the neighbourhood. The question it answers is: "given only this window, and no prior knowledge of where the continuum sits, how much signal is consistent with the data?"

From sides measures the background next door and imports it. You assert that the shoulders contain no signal and that the continuum runs straight through them into the region. The question becomes: "given the continuum is what the neighbours say it is, how much signal is consistent with the region?"

div.p: That leads to a difference worth knowing: Floating responds to peak shape, while From sides also responds to level. Under Floating a broad or uniform elevation across the region is absorbed into the continuum, so only genuinely peak-shaped excess counts as signal. Under From sides, a region that simply sits higher than its shoulders is signal, whether or not it looks Gaussian. Floating is the stricter test of "is that actually a peak?"

The failure modes are not symmetric. Floating errs toward wider limits — it can quietly absorb real signal into the continuum, so it may understate a detection. That holds while the continuum model fits; where it cannot — a curved background across a wide region — Floating overstates your confidence instead, and the paragraph below explains when. From sides errs toward wrong limits in either direction if its assumption fails: a neighbouring line, a Compton edge, a step, or curvature across the window biases the shoulders, and the limit moves with them.

Adding signal-free channels can only add information, so From sides reliably has the smaller uncertainty — but not necessarily the smaller limit, since the central value moves too, depending on whether the shoulders happen to sit high or low. A narrower number is not automatically a better one.

In practice: default to Floating — it is the best-validated mode and the defensible number when someone asks what you assumed. Reach for From sides when the region is clean and smooth for several FWHM either side, you have actually looked at the shoulders rather than trusting them, and the extra sensitivity is worth the assertion. Never use From sides with an interfering line within a few FWHM: that is exactly the case where the shoulders mislead and the method cannot notice. Note also that From sides forces a linear continuum, since four-plus-four side channels barely determine an offset and a slope. Floating does not escape that by itself — its default continuum is a straight line too — but Floating can be given a quadratic continuum, which is the option to reach for when the region visibly curves.
From sides is not a "fixed" continuum: the shoulders' own counting uncertainty is carried in the likelihood, so a weak anchor honestly widens the limit rather than pretending the continuum is known.

The deconvolution method models the background under the peak as a straight line by default. Where the true background curves noticeably across the region — wide regions, and so lower-resolution detectors — a straight line cannot follow it, and the limit comes out optimistic; the effect grows with counting time. For HPGe, regions are narrow enough that this is negligible. If the background visibly curves across your region, select the Quadratic continuum type, or narrow the region.
The Meas. time control is the dwell you are asking about, entered as a real time. It reaches the calculation two different ways:

ul.li: Under the Currie method, and under deconvolution describing the spectrum in hand, the spectrum's channel counts are projected to that real time (and its live time by the same ratio, so the dead-time fraction is preserved).

Under a background reference, the spectrum is left alone and this becomes the exposure of the future measurement being predicted — so the reference's own counting statistics are carried into the answer instead of being wished away.

div.p: Projecting the spectrum predicts the typical limit of the new measurement well; what it understates is the spread around that prediction. Scaled counts are treated as Poisson with variance equal to the scaled count, which asserts the loaded spectrum's count rate is known exactly — but the projection actually inherits that spectrum's own counting noise, and does so more heavily the further it reaches. Writing k for the entered time divided by the loaded spectrum's, measurements drawn from a real 11.5 hour background put the median projected Currie limit within 4% of what the dwell delivered across a 64-fold span of k, while the scatter about it ran about 1.6× wider than implied at k = 1 and about 4× wider at k = 16. Up to about k = 1 that is immaterial; past it, read the projection as a planning estimate rather than a bound.

The background-reference route does not scale counts, so it does not have that problem — but it covers only the deconvolution limit. A Currie limit shown beside it is still projected, and the caveat above still applies to it.

So when a measurement time is set, the result line also reports the range a measurement of that length would typically land in — the middle two thirds of the time. The quoted limit itself is not one of those trials and is not their median; it is the direct projection described above, which the measurement above puts within a few percent of the median outcome for k up to about 1. So expect the range to sit around the quoted number, but do not expect it to be centred on it exactly. The range is obtained by drawing several hundred trial measurements rather than by scaling: for each one, every channel is given a rate it could plausibly have had, given what this spectrum recorded, and then a measurement of the entered length is drawn at that rate. That accounts for the two things a plain scaling cannot — this spectrum does not pin the count rate exactly, and the future measurement will fluctuate around whatever that rate is.

The range does narrow as the planned measurement gets longer, because a longer measurement determines its own limit better. What it does not do is keep narrowing indefinitely: it settles onto a floor set by how well this spectrum pins the count rate, and no amount of future counting time can get below that. A plain scaling has no such floor — it implies the range keeps shrinking as one over the root of the time, forever. That is the difference the trials are there to capture, and it is why the quoted number is worth less as a bound the further it reaches.
It is hidden for deconvolution describing the current spectrum, where projecting the spectrum in hand and then bounding the signal in it would be circular.
You enter a real time and every reported time is a real time; the likelihood works internally in live time. A detector that reports only one of the two times is taken to have zero dead time.

The confidence levels offered include the central-normal probabilities for 1σ through 5σ — 68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73%, 99.9937%, 99.999943% — but they are applied here as one-sided confidence levels. They are offered because they are familiar numbers, not because the limit is a multiple of any sigma.

The deconvolution method's chart and its "further details" table show a quantity labelled χ2. That name is kept for continuity, but the quantity is the Cash statistic — a Poisson deviance, 2·∑(E − n + n·ln(n/E)), summed once per channel (Cash 1979). It is used in place of a Gaussian χ2 because it has no modified-Neyman variance bias and needs no variance floor for empty channels, which matters precisely in the low-count regime a detection limit lives in.

Only differences of it between trial activities are meaningful. A difference follows the same asymptotic χ2 law a Gaussian one would, and that is what sets the confidence threshold. Its absolute value does not test goodness of fit: E[statistic] is not (channels − parameters), so a χ2/DOF formed from the two numbers displayed beside each other is not a fit-quality measure and should not be read as one.

This tool reports an upper limit (or a detected value with an interval). The Currie method also computes a decision threshold Lc — the count above which you would declare a detection — and a detection limit Ld, the activity you would reliably detect. The deconvolution method does not currently provide Lc or Ld; doing so properly needs the null distribution calibrated by Monte Carlo at low counts rather than assumed, and is not yet implemented.
Uncertainties here come from counting statistics and, where applicable, the finite statistics of a background reference. Detector-response uncertainty is not propagated.
